\chapter{Reading the Greeting — One Piece at a Time}
\label{ch:zh-components}
\hlchaptermodality{2}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write each component the greeting's two characters are built from, and then assemble both characters from those pieces rather than recalling them as whole shapes.}

The second assembly, built from two components the reader wrote individually a moment earlier — and a caution that the memorable story about why it means what it means is a story, not a source.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[rén]{\zh{人} — two strokes, and a person walking}

\label{lesson:ZH-W01-ren}



\begin{quote}
You have heard Mandarin pitch. Now you meet the writing, and this book will hand it to you \textbf{one piece at a time} — never a character you have not been shown the parts of first.

This is the whole first piece:

\begin{quote}
\zh{人}
\end{quote}

Two strokes. That is the entire character.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\textbf{\zh{人}} \emph{rén} means \textbf{person}.

Look at it before you read another word about it. A stroke leaning down-left, a stroke leaning down-right, meeting at the top. \textbf{It is a figure standing on two legs, seen from the side.} You are not being asked to take that on faith — the oldest surviving forms of this character, scratched into ox bone three thousand years ago, are recognisably a standing person, and the two legs are the part that lasted.

Write it in this order, and the order is not a suggestion:

1. the \textbf{left} stroke, from the top down to the lower left — a falling sweep 2. the \textbf{right} stroke, starting near the top of the first and pressing down to the lower right

\textbf{Left before right.} Almost every character you meet will obey it, and it is worth meeting here — on a character with two strokes — rather than later on one with fifteen.

The pitch is \textbf{second tone}: \emph{rén} rises, like the end of an English question.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{人} — left stroke first, then right. Say \emph{rén} as you finish it.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{rén}, rising
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which stroke goes first — the one leaning left, or the one leaning right? (The \textbf{left}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rén (as a component)]{\zh{亻} — the same person, standing sideways}

\label{lesson:ZH-W01-ren-radical}



\begin{quote}
Write the two-stroke character for \emph{person} once, from memory. Left stroke, then right.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one character, two postures}
Every Chinese character is written inside an \textbf{evenly sized square block} — whether it has two strokes or twenty, it occupies the same footprint. That one fact drives everything you are about to see.

Because when two pieces have to share a block, one of them must get out of the way. Here is what \emph{person} looks like when it moves to the left edge to make room:

\begin{quote}
\zh{亻}
\end{quote}

Still two strokes. Still the same piece. But the wide-legged stance has been pulled upright into \textbf{one short slant on top of one long vertical}, narrow enough that something else can sit beside it.

\textbf{This is not a different character.} It is the same one, squashed. Chinese does this constantly, and the squashed forms are called \textbf{components}. When you see \zh{亻} at the left edge of a block, the character is telling you: \emph{this word is about a person.}

Write it:

1. the \textbf{short slant}, down-left, at the top 2. the \textbf{long vertical}, dropping from the middle of that slant

Top before bottom — the second of the two rules.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{人}, then \zh{亻} beside it. Notice you did not learn a new piece — you learned a new \textbf{posture}.
  \item \emph{Notice:} \zh{亻} is tall and thin because it is only using the left half of its square.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \emph{person} change shape at all? (To leave room in the square for whatever stands beside it.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U2E80.pdf}{Unicode CJK Radicals Supplement chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ěr]{\zh{尔} — a piece that is there for its sound}

\label{lesson:ZH-W01-er}



\begin{quote}
The narrow upright person — draw it once. Short slant, long vertical.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the other kind of component}
So far a component has meant something: the person piece says \emph{this is about a person.} Here is a component that works the other way.

\begin{quote}
\zh{尔}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\zh{尔}} \emph{ěr}. Five strokes: a short slant across the top, a broad cover beneath it, then a small stroke each side of a central vertical that finishes with a hook.

Now the part that matters, and it is the single most useful fact about Chinese writing:

\textbf{Most characters are built from one component pointing at the MEANING and another pointing at the SOUND.} When \zh{尔} turns up inside a character, it is usually there because the word sounds something like \emph{ěr} — not because the word has anything to do with what \zh{尔} means on its own.

That is a strange idea when your reading habits come from an alphabet, where every piece is sound and none is meaning. It is also a relief: it means characters are not arbitrary pictures to be memorised whole. They are \textbf{built}, from a small stock of pieces, and once you know the pieces you can often guess both halves of a character you have never seen.

The pitch is \textbf{third tone}: \emph{ěr} dips low.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{尔} — top slant, cover, then the middle with its hook last
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ěr}, low and dipping
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two kinds of component, then. One tells you what a word is \textbf{about}; the other tells you roughly how it \textbf{sounds}. Which kind is \zh{尔}?

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nǐ]{Putting two pieces together — and reading the result}

\label{lesson:ZH-W01-ni-build}



\begin{quote}
Two pieces, both already yours. Draw them side by side:

\begin{quote}
\zh{亻}   \zh{尔}
\end{quote}

The narrow person on the left. The five-stroke sound piece on the right.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the assembly}
Push them into one square block and you have written a character:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{亻}} + \textbf{\zh{尔}} $\to$ \textbf{\zh{你}}
\end{quote}

Read it the way you now know how to read it, half at a time:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{left} half is the person component. So this word is \textbf{about a person}.
  \item the \textbf{right} half is the sound piece \emph{ěr}. So this word \textbf{sounds something like} \emph{ěr}.
\end{itemize}

The word is \emph{nǐ}. And that is the honest state of the sound half — \emph{nǐ} and \emph{ěr} are close, not identical. \textbf{A sound component gets you into the neighbourhood, not to the door.} Sound components were chosen over two thousand years of pronunciation change, and the pronunciations moved out from under them. Expect a hint, and you will be right most of the time; expect a rule, and Chinese will embarrass you weekly.

Write it left before right, exactly as you learned each half:

1. \textbf{\zh{亻}} — short slant, long vertical 2. \textbf{\zh{尔}} — top slant, cover, then the middle and its hook

Seven strokes in total, and you did not memorise a single new one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Stop and take the measure of what just happened, because it is the reason this book teaches script this way.

You have not been shown a picture and asked to remember it. You were given two pieces, one at a time, and then shown that a character is what you get when they share a square. \textbf{The next character works the same way, and so does the one after that.} There are only a few hundred components in common use, and they recombine — which is what makes several thousand characters a climb rather than a cliff.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{你} — left half first, complete, then the right half
  \item \emph{Read it:} cover the right half. What does the left half alone tell you?
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two pieces, one block, and a character you can take apart again whenever you need to. Which half would you look at to guess the pronunciation?

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nǚ]{\zh{女} — three strokes, seated}

\label{lesson:ZH-W01-nu}



\begin{quote}
One character so far assembles from two known halves. Draw it, and name each half as you write it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
A new piece, and like the first one it is old enough to still look like what it meant:

\begin{quote}
\zh{女}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\zh{女}} \emph{nǚ} — \textbf{woman}. Three strokes.

The oracle-bone form is a \textbf{kneeling or seated figure with the arms crossed in front}. The modern character keeps the crossing: that long horizontal running right across the middle is the arms, and the two curving strokes beneath and around it are the folded body. It has straightened out over three thousand years, but nothing has been added or taken away.

Write it in this order:

1. the stroke that starts upper-right and \textbf{curves down and left} 2. the stroke that crosses it, going \textbf{down-left then flicking right} 3. the \textbf{long horizontal}, last, sweeping across both

That third stroke going last is worth noticing — a long horizontal that crosses everything else usually waits until the end.

The pitch is \textbf{third tone}, and the vowel is the rounded \emph{ü}: say \emph{ee} and then push your lips into a whistle without changing the tongue.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{女} — and let the crossing bar go last
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{nǚ}, low and dipping, lips rounded
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which stroke comes last, and why? (The \textbf{long horizontal} — a bar that crosses the whole character usually waits.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zǐ]{\zh{子} — three strokes, a child}

\label{lesson:ZH-W01-zi}



\begin{quote}
Three strokes, crossing bar last. Draw the seated figure you met a moment ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{子}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\zh{子}} \emph{zǐ} — \textbf{child}. Three strokes again, and again a figure you can still see once you are told where to look.

This one is an infant drawn \textbf{from the front}: a large head on top, two arms out to the sides, and the legs bound together so they read as one stroke rather than two. Babies were carried swaddled, and the character kept the bundle.

Write it:

1. the short stroke across the \textbf{top}, turning down — the head 2. the \textbf{vertical with a hook}, dropping through the middle — the wrapped body 3. the \textbf{horizontal} across the middle — the arms

The pitch is \textbf{third tone}. The \emph{z} is not the English \emph{z} of \emph{zoo}: it is the \emph{ds} at the end of English \emph{beds}, made with the tongue tip against the teeth.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{子} — head, hooked body, then arms
  \item \emph{Notice:} two characters now, both three strokes, both once pictures of people. Draw them side by side and compare which parts are curved.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The stroke that runs down the middle carries a hook. What part of the picture is it? (The \textbf{wrapped body and legs}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hǎo]{Two pieces again — and a warning about the story}

\label{lesson:ZH-W01-hao-build}



\begin{quote}
Both pieces are yours. Draw them side by side:

\begin{quote}
\zh{女}   \zh{子}
\end{quote}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the assembly}
Squeeze them into one block, woman on the left, child on the right:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{女}} + \textbf{\zh{子}} $\to$ \textbf{\zh{好}}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\zh{好}} \emph{hǎo}. Six strokes, three from each half, and again nothing new.

Note what is \textbf{different} about this assembly. The first one you built had a meaning half and a sound half. This one has \textbf{two meaning halves and no sound half at all} — neither piece sounds like \emph{hǎo}. Both kinds of character are common, and you cannot tell which kind you are holding until you look.

When \zh{女} is squeezed into the left of a block its long crossing bar stops short rather than sweeping past the middle, so as not to collide with what stands beside it. Same piece, narrower posture — the same accommodation you already saw the person component make.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — and a caution}]
You will find it said that \zh{好} means \emph{good} \textbf{because} a woman with a child is a good thing.

\textbf{Treat that as a story, not as evidence.} It is memorable, it is repeated everywhere, and there is no agreement among specialists that it is what happened — competing accounts read the woman as the sound half in an older pronunciation, or read the pair as a woman \emph{caring for} a child. This book will hand you an etymology when there is a source behind it and tell you plainly when there is not, and this is one of the second kind.

Use the pairing as a \textbf{memory hook}, which it genuinely is. Do not file it as a fact about why the word means what it means.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{好} — the whole left half first, then the whole right half
  \item \emph{Notice:} the crossing bar on the left half no longer sweeps all the way across. Why not?
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Six strokes, two pieces, and you built both pieces yourself. What is the one claim in this lesson you should NOT repeat as fact?

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
